paraphrase: Dhṛtarāṣṭra asks Sañjaya: in the field of dharma (dharmakṣetra), Kurukṣetra, assembled and eager to fight, what did my people (māmakāḥ) and the sons of Pāṇḍu (pāṇḍavāḥ) do?

fidelity.note: Paraphrase read against the Sanskrit: faithful, nothing added or omitted that changes the sense, no later-school or modern reading; speaker, tags and links plausible. Only verse spoken by Dhṛtarāṣṭra; speaker right; 'dharmakṣetra' kept as the text names the place.

checks.note: Verse(s) located in the local Gītā text (700-verse numbering = CE); the passage matches the paraphrase.

notes: Opening verse of the text (upakrama); the first word is 'dharmakṣetre'. Commentators read the phrase 'field of dharma' in various ways (as a traditional epithet of Kurukṣetra, or as significant for the whole teaching); the verse itself only names the place so. māmakāḥ ('my people') are Dhṛtarāṣṭra's sons; pāṇḍavāḥ are the sons of Pāṇḍu. This is the only verse of the Gītā spoken by Dhṛtarāṣṭra. Narrative framing verse: tags unmarked/general; standpoint 'ethical-social' only because the frame is the warriors' war situation.
alt_notes: The frame: the dialogue reaches Dhṛtarāṣṭra through Sañjaya's divine sight (cf. 18.75).

correction_log.new: Kṛṣṇa: out of compassion (anukampā) for them alone, I, abiding in their own being or in my own (ātma-bhāva-stha), destroy the darkness (tamas) born of ignorance (ajñāna) with the shining lamp of knowledge (jñāna-dīpa).

notes: A view the Gītā reports in order to reject it, as the view of the demonic; the verse names no school (commentators identify its holders with the Lokāyatas/materialists). The view is stated only as the view of the demonic, to be rejected; the text names no school. aparaspara-sambhūta is obscure: literally 'not arisen from one another' (i.e. not produced in an ordered causal sequence); Śaṅkara and others read it as 'arisen from the mutual union (of male and female)', which fits the following 'caused by desire'. The minimal literal sense is kept in the paraphrase. Commentators' positions are recalled, not checked against the bhāṣyas.

fidelity.note: Paraphrase keeps the verse's own words ('abandoning all dharmas', 'go to me alone for refuge', 'I will release you from all sins', 'do not grieve'); the Advaita, Viśiṣṭādvaita and other readings only in labelled notes; prapatti ids deliberately not linked, dsp:is-prapatti-an-upaya linked at the locus its Viśiṣṭādvaita side cites.

Rāmānuja's two readings (giving up agency and fruit while performing the dharmas; or, with "athavā", refuge in place of the expiations for one unable to begin bhakti-yoga) were located.

notes: The verse does not say which dharmas are to be abandoned or in what sense (A). 'mā śucaḥ' closes the teaching that began with 'you grieve for those not to be grieved for' (2.11) and echoes 16.5; 'śaraṇaṃ vraja' answers Arjuna's 'tvāṃ prapannam' (2.7), and 'all dharmas' his 'dharma-saṃmūḍha-cetāḥ' (2.7) (B). 18.64 marks this word, with 18.65, as 'the most secret of all'. 'mokṣayiṣyāmi' is 'I will release', its object being 'from all sins'. The commentators divide sharply on 'sarva-dharmān parityajya': renouncing all actions, dharma and adharma alike, in favour of knowledge of the one self (Śaṅkara); giving up the sense of agency, possession and fruit in all dharmas, or — for one unable to begin bhakti-yoga — taking refuge in place of the other means and expiations (Rāmānuja); giving up the sense of agency and attachment while still doing one's duties (other readings). In the Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition the verse is the carama-śloka (data/ trm:carama-sloka), the charter of prapatti. cpt:prapatti and trm:prapatti are deliberately not linked: the verse has no form of pra-√pad, and those data/ entries define the Śrīvaiṣṇava doctrine; the verse is linked in the Gītā's own terms (cpt:surrender-to-the-lord, prc:saranagati, trm:sarana, trm:saranagati) and to dsp:is-prapatti-an-upaya, whose Viśiṣṭādvaita side cites it. How the traditions read it for the purport of the whole text is recorded in dsp:gita-primary-teaching and the notes of tea:bhagavad-gita:thesis. The paraphrase keeps the verse's own words. Commentators' positions are recalled, not checked against the bhāṣyas.
alt_notes: The 'carama śloka' (final verse) of the Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition. Readings: renounce all works and rest in knowledge of the self non-different from the Lord (Śaṅkara); give up the sense of doership in the means, or — for those unable to practise bhakti-yoga — take refuge as the means (Rāmānuja's alternative readings); surrender as the sole means (later Śrīvaiṣṇava teaching on prapatti).

The new wording gives the literal sense (what is not / what is; being / non-being) with both glosses of asat and sat — the minimal shared sense, with no school's reading imported.

checks.note: Verse(s) located in the local Gītā text (700-verse numbering = CE); the passage matches the paraphrase.

notes: Much-disputed verse. The commentators identify the asat and the sat differently (e.g. the body and the pairs of opposites of 2.14 as asat and the self or Brahman as sat), divide on whether the verse speaks of existence or of reality, and read 'anta' as 'conclusion, final determination' or as 'boundary, distinction'. Later schools cite it in the debates on causation (satkārya) and on the status of the world. The verse itself states only the principle and that the seers of reality have seen it.
alt_notes: Cited in config/principles.md as the example of a 'bridging' passage. Advaita reads sat/asat as the real self and the unreal world; other schools read it as the imperishable self and the perishable body.

fidelity.note: Fixed: 'paramātmā samāhitaḥ' had been rendered 'the supreme self is composed', adopting one construal although the note said the paraphrase does not decide; both construals now given; jitātman rendered reflexively.

correction_log.old: Kṛṣṇa: for one who has conquered the self and is at peace (praśānta), the supreme self (paramātman) is composed (samāhita) amid cold and heat, pleasure and pain, honour and dishonour.
correction_log.new: Kṛṣṇa: for one who has conquered himself (jitātman) and is at peace (praśānta), amid cold and heat, pleasure and pain, honour and dishonour, 'paramātmā samāhitaḥ' — either the supreme self (paramātman) is established (samāhita), or, taking 'param' adverbially, his self is supremely composed.
correction_log.reason: 'paramātmā samāhitaḥ' was rendered 'the supreme self is composed', deciding a disputed construal although the entry's note says the paraphrase does not decide; both construals are now given; 'conquered the self' made reflexive (jitātman).

notes: The construal is disputed: 'paramātmā samāhitaḥ' may mean that the supreme self is present and established in him (realized as his self), or, taking 'param' adverbially, that his self is supremely composed; the paraphrase gives both construals without deciding.

paraphrase: Kṛṣṇa: all these are noble (udāra), but the knower I hold to be my very self (ātmā eva me matam); for he, yoked in himself (yuktātmā), is established in me alone as the unsurpassed goal.
speaker: Kṛṣṇa
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted

fidelity.note: Fixed: 'yuktātmā' had been rendered 'with self yoked' (reflexive ātman read as 'the self'); now 'yoked in himself'. 'ātmaiva me matam' is kept as 'my very self' with both readings (identity / dear as his own self) in notes; no school's reading imported.

correction_log.old: Kṛṣṇa: all these are noble (udāra), but the knower I hold to be my very self (ātmā eva me matam); for he, with self yoked (yuktātmā), is established in me alone as the unsurpassed goal.
correction_log.new: Kṛṣṇa: all these are noble (udāra), but the knower I hold to be my very self (ātmā eva me matam); for he, yoked in himself (yuktātmā), is established in me alone as the unsurpassed goal.
correction_log.reason: 'yuktātmā' was rendered 'with self yoked', which reads the reflexive ātman of the compound as 'the self'; it is the knower himself (his own person/mind) who is yoked.

notes: 'jñānī tv ātmaiva me matam' is read by commentators as the knower's identity with the Lord (the knower is his very self) or as the knower being as dear to him as his own self, his support or very life; the verse says only that the Lord 'holds' (matam) the knower to be his self, and the paraphrase keeps the words 'my very self'. The other three kinds are still called noble (udāra: generous, exalted).

paraphrase: Chapter 1 sets the scene and the crisis. 1.1: Dhṛtarāṣṭra asks Sañjaya what the two assembled armies did at Kurukṣetra, 'the field of dharma'. 1.2–11: Duryodhana goes to his teacher Droṇa, lists the leading warriors of the Pāṇḍava army (1.4–6) and of his own (1.8–9), compares the two forces (1.10) and orders that Bhīṣma be guarded (1.11). 1.12–19: Bhīṣma and then the Pāṇḍava side (Kṛṣṇa, Arjuna, Bhīma, Yudhiṣṭhira, Nakula, Sahadeva and others) blow their named conches; the uproar rends the Kauravas' hearts. 1.20–27: Arjuna asks Kṛṣṇa to station the chariot between the armies; Kṛṣṇa does so and tells him to look at the assembled Kurus; Arjuna sees his elders, teachers and kin on both sides. 1.28–46: overcome by pity (kṛpā) and despair (viṣāda), Arjuna describes his bodily collapse (1.28–30), says he sees no good (śreyas) in killing kin and wants neither victory nor kingship (1.31–37), argues that destroying a family destroys the family dharmas, leads to varṇa-mixture, the fall of the ancestors and hell (1.38–44), and says it would be better to be killed unresisting (1.45–46). 1.47: Arjuna sits down in the chariot, casting away his bow, his mind overwhelmed by grief (śoka). The chapter's purpose, as it presents itself, is to state Arjuna's grief and his argument from family dharma, which the following teaching answers.

paraphrase: Chapter 10 is the Lord's account of his manifestations (vibhūti), in four movements. (1) 10.1–11: the Lord resumes his supreme word, spoken out of a wish for Arjuna's welfare to him who takes delight (prīyamāṇa) (10.1); neither the gods nor the great seers know his origin, for he is their beginning (10.2); whoever knows him as unborn, without beginning, the great lord of the world, is undeluded and freed from all sins (10.3); the states of beings, from understanding and knowledge to fame and ill-fame, arise from him alone (10.4–5), and the seven great seers of old and the four Manus (or: the seven great seers, the four of old and the Manus), sharing his being, were born of mind, and from them come the world's creatures (10.6); whoever knows this vibhūti and yoga of his in truth is joined with unwavering yoga (10.7); knowing him as the origin of all, the wise worship him, their thought on him, awakening one another and speaking of him, content and delighting (10.8–9); to these, ever yoked and worshipping with love, he gives the yoga of understanding by which they come to him, and out of compassion he destroys their darkness born of ignorance with the lamp of knowledge (10.10–11). (2) 10.12–18: Arjuna acknowledges him as the supreme brahman, the supreme abode, the supreme purifier, the eternal divine Person, as all the seers — Nārada, Asita Devala and Vyāsa — declare and as he himself says (10.12–13); neither gods nor dānavas know his manifestation, and he alone knows himself by himself (10.14–15); Arjuna asks to be told his divine manifestations in full and in which things he is to be contemplated (10.16–18). (3) 10.19–39: the Lord names his manifestations by the principal ones, since there is no end to them (10.19): first the self seated in all beings and the beginning, middle and end of beings (10.20), then the pre-eminent member of class after class — gods, seers, Vedas, the mind among the senses, sentience in beings, the one syllable, japa among sacrifices, time, death, the letter a, silence, knowledge and the rest (10.21–38) — and last the seed of all beings, without which nothing moving or unmoving could exist (10.39). (4) 10.40–42: there is no end to his divine manifestations and this has been only an indication; whatever being is glorious or mighty has arisen from a portion of his splendour; and he stands supporting this whole world with a single portion. Purpose, as the chapter presents it: that Arjuna, who takes delight (10.1) and is never sated with hearing (10.18), may know the Lord's vibhūti and yoga in truth (10.1, 10.7) and have supports for contemplating him in all things (10.17, 10.41).

paraphrase: Chapter 11 is the vision of the Lord's sovereign, universal form, in eight movements. (1) 11.1–4: Arjuna says his delusion is gone through the supreme secret called adhyātma spoken out of favour to him, and that he has heard in detail of the arising and passing of beings and of the Lord's imperishable greatness; he accepts what the Lord has said of himself and asks, if the Lord thinks him able, to see his sovereign form. (2) 11.5–8: the Lord bids him behold his manifold divine forms by hundreds and thousands, the gods and many wonders, and the whole world standing as one in his body; since Arjuna cannot see him with his own eye, he gives him a divine eye to behold his sovereign yoga. (3) 11.9–14: Sañjaya tells Dhṛtarāṣṭra of the form Hari showed: many mouths and eyes, divine ornaments, garlands and raised weapons, facing every way, its light like a thousand suns risen at once; the whole world, divided in many ways, standing as one in the body of the god of gods; Arjuna, amazed, his hair on end, bows and speaks. (4) 11.15–31: Arjuna describes what he sees — the gods, Brahmā, the seers and all hosts of beings in the form; no end, middle or beginning; the imperishable, the supreme to be known, the resting-place of the universe, the guardian of eternal dharma; then the fierce form at which the worlds and he himself are shaken, into whose flaming mouths the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Karṇa and the warriors of his own side rush like rivers into the ocean and moths into a flame — and asks who this fierce one is. (5) 11.32–34: the Lord answers: 'I am Time, grown mighty, maker of the destruction of the worlds'; even without Arjuna the warriors will cease to be; they are already slain by him; Arjuna is to rise, be merely the instrument, and fight. (6) 11.35–46: trembling, Arjuna bows and praises him (11.36–40) — greater than all, the imperishable, being and non-being and what is beyond, the first god, pervading all and therefore all — asks forgiveness for past familiarity (11.41–44), and, thrilled and afraid, asks to see again the crowned, four-armed form (11.45–46). (7) 11.47–51: the Lord says he showed this form, never seen before by another, out of grace and by his own yoga, and that it cannot be seen by Vedas, sacrifice, study, gifts, rites or austerities; he bids Arjuna not fear, shows again his own gentle form, and Arjuna is restored to himself. (8) 11.52–55: the form is hard to see, even the gods long to see it; not by Vedas, austerity, giving or sacrifice, but by undivided devotion alone can the Lord be known, seen in truth and entered; whoever does his work, holds him supreme, is devoted, unattached and without enmity toward any being comes to him. Purpose, as the chapter presents it: to grant the sight Arjuna asked for (11.3–4), to reveal the Lord as Time who has already decided the battle (11.32–34), and to state the means by which he is seen and reached (11.54–55).

paraphrase: Chapter 12 answers which worshippers know yoga best and sets out the practice of devotion, in six movements. (1) 12.1: Arjuna asks which know yoga best — the devotees who, ever yoked in the way just described (11.55), worship the Lord, or those who worship the imperishable, the unmanifest. (2) 12.2–5: the Lord answers that those who fix the mind on him and worship him, ever yoked, with supreme faith, he holds to be the most yoked; those who worship the imperishable — indefinable, unmanifest, all-pervading, unthinkable, unchanging, immovable, constant — restraining the senses, even in understanding everywhere and delighting in the welfare of all beings, also reach him; but their hardship is greater, for the unmanifest goal is reached with difficulty by the embodied. (3) 12.6–7: those who resign all actions to him and, holding him supreme, worship him meditating with undivided yoga, he before long delivers from the ocean of death and saṃsāra. (4) 12.8–12: graded instruction — fix mind and understanding on him alone and you will dwell in him; if the thought cannot be held steady, seek him by the yoga of practice; if unable even to practise, be intent on work for him; if unable even that, taking refuge in his yoga and self-restrained, give up the fruit of all actions; then a ranking — knowledge better than practice, meditation superior to knowledge, relinquishing the fruit of actions superior to meditation, peace following immediately on relinquishment. (5) 12.13–19: the marks of the devotee dear to the Lord — hating no being, friendly and compassionate, without 'mine' and 'I', the same in pain and pleasure, forbearing, content, self-restrained, firm in resolve, mind and understanding offered to him; neither disturbing nor disturbed by the world, free of elation, intolerance, fear and agitation; without expectation, pure, capable, impartial, relinquishing every undertaking; neither rejoicing nor hating, grieving nor craving, having given up good and bad; the same toward enemy and friend, in honour and dishonour, cold and heat, blame and praise; silent, content with whatever comes, homeless, steady in judgement, full of devotion — each group closing with 'he is dear to me'. (6) 12.20: those who with faith, holding him supreme, attend to this nectar of dharma as spoken, are exceedingly dear to him. Purpose, as the chapter presents it: to answer which worshippers are the best knowers of yoga (12.1–2) and to lay out graded means and the marks of the devotee (12.8–20).

The next verse, 13.1, is the extra verse of this edition (Arjuna's question about prakṛti and puruṣa, the field and its knower); 13.1 in the cross-references is this edition's numbering and has no counterpart in the 700-verse text.

paraphrase: Chapter 13 (35 verses in this edition, whose first verse is the extra verse found in some editions; 34 in the 700-verse numbering, which runs one lower from 13.2) distinguishes the field (kṣetra) from its knower (kṣetrajña). Movements: 13.1 Arjuna asks about prakṛti and puruṣa, the field and its knower, knowledge and the knowable. 13.2–5 Kṛṣṇa calls the body the field and the one who knows it the knower of the field, declares himself also the knower in all fields, calls the knowledge of both 'knowledge', and says the subject has been sung by the seers, in the metres and in the brahmasūtra words. 13.6–7 the field is listed with its modifications (the great elements, the sense of 'I', understanding, the unmanifest, the ten faculties and the one, the five domains of the senses, desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, the aggregate, sentience, steadiness). 13.8–12 twenty dispositions, from absence of pride to keeping in view the aim of the knowledge of reality, are declared 'knowledge'; what is other than them is ignorance. 13.13–19 the knowable: the beginningless supreme brahman, said to be neither being nor non-being, with hands, feet and eyes everywhere, without guṇas yet their experiencer, inside and outside beings, undivided yet as if divided, the light of lights, set in the heart of all; the field, knowledge and the knowable having been told, the devotee who knows this becomes fit for Kṛṣṇa's state. 13.20–24 prakṛti and puruṣa are both beginningless; prakṛti is the cause in agency, puruṣa in experiencing; attachment to the guṇas causes births in good and bad wombs; the highest puruṣa in the body is the onlooker, consenter, supporter, experiencer and great lord, and is called the supreme self; one who knows this is not born again. 13.25–26 some see the self by meditation, others by the yoga of sāṃkhya, others by the yoga of action; others worship on hearing from others, and they too cross death. 13.27–35 every being is born from the union of field and knower; one who sees the supreme lord the same in all beings, sees prakṛti as the doer of actions and one's self as not the doer, and sees the separate existence of beings as resting in the one, truly sees and attains brahman; the supreme self, beginningless and without guṇas, neither acts nor is stained though in the body, as all-pervading space is not stained; as the one sun lights the whole world, the possessor of the field lights the whole field; those who know the difference between field and knower with the eye of knowledge go to the supreme. The purpose the chapter states: knowledge of the field and its knower and of their difference (13.3, 13.35).

paraphrase: Chapter 14 (27 verses) sets out the three guṇas and the way beyond them. Movements: 14.1–2 Kṛṣṇa announces again the highest knowledge, by which all the sages reached the highest perfection and came to have the same nature (sādharmya) as his, not born at creation nor troubled at dissolution. 14.3–4 the great brahman is his womb; he places the embryo in it and is the seed-giving father of all forms. 14.5–10 sattva, rajas and tamas, born of prakṛti, bind the embodied one — sattva by attachment to happiness and knowledge, rajas by attachment to action, tamas by heedlessness, idleness and sleep — and each prevails by overpowering the other two. 14.11–13 the signs of each when increased. 14.14–15 where one goes on dying in each. 14.16–18 their fruits, and the upward, middle and downward courses of those who abide in them. 14.19–20 one who sees no agent but the guṇas and knows what is higher than them attains Kṛṣṇa's state, and the embodied one who goes beyond the three guṇas attains the immortal, freed from birth, death, old age and pain. 14.21 Arjuna asks the marks, the conduct and the means of one gone beyond the guṇas. 14.22–25 the marks and conduct: not hating or longing for the guṇas' effects, unshaken, knowing only 'the guṇas are operating', the same in pleasure and pain, blame and praise, honour and dishonour, toward friend and foe, relinquishing all undertakings. 14.26–27 the means: one who serves Kṛṣṇa with the unswerving yoga of devotion goes beyond the guṇas and becomes fit for becoming brahman — for he is the foundation of brahman, of the immortal and imperishable, of everlasting dharma and of absolute happiness. The purpose the chapter states: the highest knowledge (14.1–2) — how the guṇas bind and the way beyond them (14.5, 14.19–26).

paraphrase: Chapter 15 (20 verses) moves from the world-tree to the highest person. Movements: 15.1–2 the imperishable aśvattha with roots above and branches below, its leaves the metres, its branches swollen by the guṇas with the sense-objects as shoots, its roots below bound up with action in the human world; to know it is to know the Veda. 15.3–6 its form, end, beginning and foundation are not perceived here; it is to be cut with the weapon of non-attachment and the place of no return sought, with the words 'I take refuge in that primal person'; those free of pride, delusion, attachment and desire, intent on what pertains to the self and released from the pairs reach that imperishable place, unlit by sun, moon or fire, Kṛṣṇa's supreme abode. 15.7–11 an eternal portion of Kṛṣṇa, become the living being, draws the senses and mind, carries them from body to body as wind carries scents, and enjoys objects through them; the deluded do not see it, those with the eye of knowledge and striving yogins do. 15.12–15 Kṛṣṇa is the radiance in sun, moon and fire, sustains beings, nourishes plants as soma, digests food as vaiśvānara, is seated in the heart of all, the source of memory, knowledge and removal (apohana), the one to be known by all the Vedas, maker of the vedānta and knower of the Veda. 15.16–20 there are two persons in the world, the perishable (all beings) and the imperishable (the one standing firm), and the highest person, another, called the supreme self, the imperishable lord; Kṛṣṇa, beyond the perishable and higher than the imperishable, is the puruṣottama; one who knows him so knows all and worships him with his whole being; this is the most secret teaching, understanding which one is wise and has done what is to be done. The purpose the chapter states: to make known the puruṣottama (15.18–20).

paraphrase: Chapter 16 (Kṛṣṇa to Arjuna; no question opens it). Structure: (1) 16.1–3 the divine endowment (daivī sampad), twenty-six qualities from fearlessness to absence of excessive pride; (2) 16.4 the demonic endowment (āsurī sampad): hypocrisy, arrogance, excessive pride, anger, harshness, ignorance; (3) 16.5 their results — release and bondage — and the assurance to Arjuna that he is born to the divine one ('do not grieve'); (4) 16.6–20 the two creations of beings and a long portrait of the demonic: their not knowing engagement and withdrawal (pravṛtti, nivṛtti) and their lack of purity, conduct and truth (16.7), their view that the world is without truth, foundation or Lord and caused by desire (16.8), their destructive deeds, insatiable desire, anxiety and unjust getting (16.9–12), their boasting inner speech (16.13–15), their fall into hell (16.16), their sacrifices in name only and hatred of the Lord in all bodies (16.17–18), and the Lord's casting them into demonic wombs birth after birth, down to the lowest state (16.19–20); (5) 16.21–22 desire, anger and greed as the threefold gate of hell, freedom from which leads to the highest goal; (6) 16.23–24 whoever sets aside the ordinance of scripture attains neither perfection, happiness nor the highest goal, so scripture is the authority for what is to be done. Purpose, as the chapter presents it: to distinguish the two endowments by their results, reassure Arjuna, and direct him to act by the authority of scripture.

paraphrase: Chapter 17 (Arjuna asks; Kṛṣṇa answers). Structure: (1) 17.1 Arjuna asks about those who sacrifice with faith but set aside the ordinance of scripture — is their standing sattva, rajas or tamas? (2) 17.2–6 faith is threefold, born of one's nature; the person is made of faith; the sāttvic worship the gods, the rājasic yakṣas and rākṣasas, the tāmasic the departed and spirits; those who practise terrible austerity outside scripture, tormenting the body and the Lord within it, are of demonic resolve; (3) 17.7–22 food, sacrifice, austerity and giving are each threefold: food (17.8–10); sacrifice (17.11–13); austerity of body, speech and mind (17.14–16) and its three kinds (17.17–19); giving (17.20–22); (4) 17.23–28 '[oṃ] tat sat' (this edition's 17.23 lacks oṃ) is the threefold designation of brahman: rites begin with oṃ, acts are done without aiming at fruit with 'tat' by seekers of release, 'sat' is said of being, goodness, praiseworthy acts and steadfastness in them; what is done without faith is 'asat' and worthless here and hereafter. Purpose, as the chapter presents it: to answer Arjuna's question by showing that faith and every act follow the guṇas, that the sāttvic form is done as duty without desire for fruit, and that faith is indispensable.

paraphrase: Chapter 18 (Arjuna asks; Kṛṣṇa teaches; Arjuna answers; Sañjaya closes). Structure: (1) 18.1 Arjuna asks the truth of renunciation (saṃnyāsa) and relinquishment (tyāga); (2) 18.2–12 two definitions reported from the wise, two opposed views on giving up action (18.3), and Kṛṣṇa's conclusion: sacrifice, giving and austerity are not to be given up but done without attachment and fruit; relinquishment is threefold; since the embodied cannot give up action entirely, the relinquisher is the one who gives up the fruit; (3) 18.13–17 the five causes of action (declared in the sāṃkhya) and the one whose disposition is not shaped by the sense of 'I', who does not slay and is not bound; (4) 18.18–40 the threefold impulse and composition of action and the guṇa-classification of knowledge, action, agent, understanding, steadfastness and happiness, closing with the statement that no being is free of the guṇas; (5) 18.41–48 the duties of the four classes from their own nature, perfection by worshipping with one's own work, the priority of one's own dharma; (6) 18.49–56 the sequence from unattached understanding and naiṣkarmya-siddhi through the discipline that makes one fit for becoming brahman, to supreme devotion, knowing and entering the Lord, and the eternal abode by grace for one who acts while taking refuge in him; (7) 18.57–66 direct commands to Arjuna: renounce all actions to me in thought, your nature will make you fight in any case, the Lord in the heart moves all beings, take refuge in him; then the most secret word: be one whose mind is on me, my devotee, one who sacrifices to me, bow to me (18.65); abandoning all dharmas, go to me alone for refuge; I will release you from all sins; do not grieve (18.66); (8) 18.67–71 who may and may not be told the teaching, and the fruit of teaching, studying and hearing it; (9) 18.72–73 Kṛṣṇa's question whether the delusion is gone and Arjuna's reply that it is, that memory is regained, and that he will do Kṛṣṇa's word; (10) 18.74–78 Sañjaya's close: the wondrous dialogue heard by Vyāsa's grace, his repeated joy, and his conviction that fortune and victory are where Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna are. Purpose, as the chapter presents it: the truth of saṃnyāsa and tyāga asked in 18.1 (answered in 18.2–12 and taken up again at 18.49 and 18.57), the word it calls 'the most secret of all' (18.64–66), and the removal of Arjuna's delusion, which the teacher checks and the disciple confirms (18.72–73).

paraphrase: Chapter 2 opens the teaching. 2.1–10 (frame): Kṛṣṇa rebukes Arjuna's faintness and unmanliness (2.2–3); Arjuna restates his dilemma — he cannot fight Bhīṣma and Droṇa, would rather live on alms, does not know which outcome is better — and asks Kṛṣṇa, as his disciple who has come for refuge, to tell him for certain what is better (śreyas) (2.4–8); he says 'I will not fight' and falls silent, and Kṛṣṇa, as if smiling, answers (2.9–10). 2.11–30: the teaching on the embodied self (dehin): the wise do not grieve; the self was never not and will never cease; it passes through bodies as through the ages of life and as through garments; what is not (asat) has no being and what is (sat) no non-being; the self neither slays nor is slain, is unborn, eternal, uncuttable, unmanifest and unthinkable; even on the contrary view birth and death are inevitable; therefore do not grieve. 2.31–38: the argument from one's own dharma (svadharma) and honour: a dharmic battle is the kṣatriya's best good and a door to heaven, refusal brings sin and disgrace; fight treating pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat alike. 2.39: transition — the understanding (buddhi) given 'in sāṃkhya' is now given 'in yoga'. 2.40–53: the yoga of understanding (buddhi-yoga): resolute understanding is one (2.41); the flowery speech of those who delight in Vedic statements and seek heaven and power keeps understanding from samādhi; the Vedas concern the three guṇas, be free of them (2.42–46); your right is to action, not its fruits; yoga is sameness and skill in actions; the wise, yoked with understanding, abandon the fruit and are freed from the bondage of birth (2.47–51); when understanding passes beyond delusion and stands steady in samādhi, you will attain yoga (2.52–53). 2.54–72: Arjuna asks about the person of steady wisdom (sthitaprajña); Kṛṣṇa describes him: he gives up all desires and is content in the self, unshaken by sorrow and pleasure, free from passion, fear and anger, withdraws the senses like a tortoise (2.55–61); the chain from dwelling on objects through attachment, desire, anger, delusion and loss of memory to ruin (2.62–63), and its reverse through mastered senses to serenity and steady understanding (2.64–68); the sage is awake where beings sleep, is filled by desires like the ocean yet unmoved, and without 'mine' and 'I' attains peace (2.69–71); this is the brahmic state, reaching which even at death one attains brahma-nirvāṇa (2.72). The chapter's purpose, as it presents itself, is to answer Arjuna's grief and his request for the good, first by knowledge of the self, then by the discipline of action done with steady understanding, culminating in the portrait of the one whose wisdom is steady.

paraphrase: Chapter 3 answers the question of understanding versus action. 3.1–2: Arjuna asks why, if understanding (buddhi) is held superior to action, Kṛṣṇa urges him to terrible action, and asks for one decisive teaching. 3.3–9: Kṛṣṇa says he declared of old a twofold commitment (niṣṭhā) — the yoga of knowledge for the sāṃkhyas and the yoga of action for the yogins; actionlessness (naiṣkarmya) is not reached by not acting nor perfection by mere renunciation; no one can stay without acting, since the guṇas of prakṛti make everyone act; restraining the organs of action while the mind dwells on objects is hypocrisy, while karma-yoga with the senses controlled and without attachment excels; do your allotted action, for the world is bound by action except action for sacrifice. 3.10–16: Prajāpati created beings with sacrifice, telling them to nourish the gods and be nourished; who enjoys the gods' gifts without offering is a thief; eating the remains of sacrifice frees from fault; the wheel of food, rain, sacrifice, action, brahman and the imperishable must be kept turning. 3.17–18: for one who delights and is content in the self there is nothing that must be done. 3.19–26: therefore act unattached; Janaka and others reached perfection by action; act for the holding together of the world (loka-saṃgraha), since people follow the best; Kṛṣṇa himself, needing nothing, keeps acting lest the worlds perish; the wise should act unattached as the unwise act attached, and not unsettle the understanding of the ignorant. 3.27–29: actions are done by the guṇas, and only one deluded by the sense of 'I' (ahaṃkāra) thinks 'I am the doer'; the knower of the truth is not attached. 3.30–32: resign all actions to Kṛṣṇa and fight; those who follow this teaching with faith are released, those who cavil are lost. 3.33–35: all beings follow their nature; attraction and aversion lie in wait in the sense-objects; one's own dharma, though imperfect, is better than another's. 3.36–43: Arjuna asks what drives a person to sin against his will; Kṛṣṇa names desire and anger, born of rajas, the enemy that covers knowledge as smoke covers fire, seated in the senses, mind and understanding; restrain the senses first, know what is beyond understanding, steady the self by the self and slay desire. The chapter's purpose, as it presents itself, is to show why Arjuna must act — action being unavoidable, sacrificial, exemplary and non-binding when done without attachment — and to name desire as what must be overcome.

actionlessness (naiṣkarmya) is not reached by not acting nor perfection by mere renunciation; no one can stay without acting, since the guṇas of prakṛti make everyone act; restraining the organs of action while the mind dwells on objects is hypocrisy, while karma-yoga with the senses controlled and without attachment excels; do your allotted action, for the world is bound by action except action for sacrifice. 3.10–16: Prajāpati created beings with sacrifice, telling them to nourish the gods and be nourished; who enjoys the gods' gifts without offering is a thief; eating the remains of sacrifice frees from fault; the wheel of food, rain, sacrifice, action, brahman and the imperishable must be kept turning. 3.17–18: for one who delights and is content in the self there is nothing that must be done. 3.19–26: therefore act unattached; Janaka and others reached perfection by action; act for the holding together of the world (loka-saṃgraha), since people follow the best; Kṛṣṇa himself, needing nothing, keeps acting lest the worlds perish; the wise should act unattached as the unwise act attached, and not unsettle the understanding of the ignorant. 3.27–29: actions are done by the guṇas, and only the ego-deluded thinks 'I am the doer'; the knower of the truth is not attached. 3.30–32: resign all actions to Kṛṣṇa and fight; those who follow this teaching with faith are released, those who cavil are lost. 3.33–35: all beings follow their nature; attraction and aversion lie in wait in the sense-objects; one's own dharma, though imperfect, is better than another's. 3.36–43: Arjuna asks what drives a person to sin against his will; Kṛṣṇa names desire and anger, born of rajas, the enemy that covers knowledge as smoke covers fire, seated in the senses, mind and understanding; restrain the senses first, know what is beyond understanding, steady the self by the self and slay desire. The chapter's purpose, as it presents itself, is to show why Arjuna must act — action being unavoidable, sacrificial, exemplary and non-binding when done without attachment — and to name desire as what must be overcome.

notes: The colophon title (commonly 'Karmayoga' in the vulgate) is not among this edition's segments. 4.1–3 immediately present the yoga just taught as an ancient teaching handed down from Vivasvat (to Manu and Ikṣvāku).

paraphrase: Chapter 4 moves in six steps. (1) 4.1–3: the Lord declares that he taught this imperishable yoga to Vivasvat, who told it to Manu, and Manu to Ikṣvāku; known by the royal sages through succession, it was lost over a long time, and he now teaches the same ancient yoga to Arjuna because he is his devotee and friend — it is the highest secret. (2) 4.4–10: to Arjuna's question how he could have taught it to Vivasvat, who was born earlier, the Lord answers that he knows his many births and Arjuna's; though unborn and lord of beings, he comes into being by his own māyā whenever dharma declines, to protect the good, destroy wrongdoers and establish dharma, age after age; whoever knows his divine birth and action is not reborn but comes to him, as many have, purified by the austerity of knowledge. (3) 4.11–15: he receives people in the way they approach him; those who want quick success of their actions sacrifice to the deities; he made the fourfold class order by the division of guṇa and action, yet is a non-doer, unstained by action; knowing this the ancient seekers of liberation acted, so Arjuna should act. (4) 4.16–23: what action, wrong action (vikarma) and inaction are; the wise one sees inaction in action and action in inaction; free of desire and intention, his actions burnt in the fire of knowledge, unattached to the fruit, he is not bound though acting, and for one who acts for the sake of sacrifice action dissolves. (5) 4.24–32: action as sacrifice — every element of the offering is Brahman — and a list of the many kinds of sacrifice (to the gods; sacrifice offered into the fire of Brahman; the senses into the fires of restraint; the sense-objects into the fires of the senses; the actions of the senses and of breath into the fire of self-restraint; sacrifice of material things, austerity, yoga, recitation and knowledge; prāṇa and apāna offered into each other; breaths into breaths by those regulated in food), all born of action and all destroying impurity. (6) 4.33–42: the sacrifice of knowledge is better, since all action culminates in knowledge; knowledge is to be learned from seers of the truth by prostration, questioning and service; it is a raft over all wrongdoing, a fire that burns all actions, the supreme purifier, gained by the faithful and self-restrained and bringing supreme peace, while the ignorant, faithless doubter perishes; actions do not bind one who has renounced action by yoga and cut doubt by knowledge; the chapter ends: cut this doubt with the sword of knowledge, resort to yoga and stand up. Purpose, as the chapter presents it: to ground the teaching in an ancient transmission and in the Lord who gives it, and to show that action done as sacrifice, without attachment and with knowledge, does not bind and culminates in knowledge, so that Arjuna may act free of doubt.

paraphrase: Chapter 5 moves in seven steps. (1) 5.1: Arjuna asks which is better, the renunciation of actions (saṃnyāsa) or yoga, since Kṛṣṇa praises both. (2) 5.2–6: both lead to the highest good, but the yoga of action is superior to the renunciation of action; the constant renouncer is the one who neither hates nor desires; only the childish, not the learned, call Sāṃkhya and Yoga separate, since the same place is reached by both; renunciation is hard to attain without yoga, while the sage yoked in yoga soon reaches Brahman. (3) 5.7–12: the one yoked in yoga, whose self has become the self of all beings, is not stained though acting; the yoked knower of reality thinks 'I do nothing', holding that the senses move among their objects; one who acts placing actions in Brahman and abandoning attachment is unstained, like a lotus leaf by water; yogins act for the purification of the self; the yoked one who gives up the fruit attains lasting peace, while the unyoked, attached to the fruit through desire, is bound. (4) 5.13–17: the embodied one, having renounced all actions with the mind, dwells at ease in the city of nine gates, neither acting nor causing action; the master (prabhu) creates neither agency nor actions nor their link with the fruit — inherent nature (svabhāva) acts; knowledge is covered by ignorance and so creatures are deluded, but where ignorance is destroyed by knowledge, knowledge illumines the highest like the sun, and those intent on That go to non-return. (5) 5.18–26: the learned see the same in all beings; those whose mind rests in sameness conquer creation here and are established in Brahman, which is flawless and the same; the knower of Brahman is unmoved by the pleasant and the unpleasant; unattached to external contacts he finds the happiness that is in the self, for contact-born enjoyments are wombs of sorrow; one who withstands the surge of desire and anger is yoked and happy; the yogin with happiness, delight and light within, having become Brahman, attains brahma-nirvāṇa, which lies near the self-knowing ascetics free of desire and anger. (6) 5.27–28: in outline, a practice (external contacts put outside, the gaze between the brows, prāṇa and apāna made even) of the sage intent on liberation, who is ever free. (7) 5.29: knowing the Lord as enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, great lord of all the worlds and friend of all beings, one attains peace. Purpose, as the chapter presents it: to answer the question of renunciation versus the yoga of action by showing that true renunciation is inward, that the two reach the same goal, and that the goal is brahma-nirvāṇa and peace.

paraphrase: Chapter 6 moves in nine steps. (1) 6.1–4: the one who does the action that is to be done without depending on its fruit is both renouncer and yogin, not one who merely gives up the sacred fires and rites; what is called renunciation is yoga, for no one becomes a yogin without renouncing intention (saṅkalpa); for the sage wishing to ascend to yoga action is the means, for the one who has ascended calm (śama) is the means, and he has ascended when he is attached neither to sense-objects nor to actions. (2) 6.5–9: one should raise the self by the self, which is its own friend or enemy; for the self-conquered and tranquil, amid the pairs of opposites, the supreme self (paramātman) is established — or, on the other construal, his self is supremely composed; the yoked yogin, satisfied with knowledge and realized knowledge, sees clod, stone and gold alike and is even in intellect (sama-buddhi) toward friend and foe, the good and the wicked. (3) 6.10–17: instruction in meditation — solitude, a firm seat in a clean place, the mind (manas) made one-pointed, body, head and neck held in line, the gaze toward the nose-tip, fearlessness, the vow of the brahmacārin, the mind (manas) restrained, thought (citta) on the Lord and intent on him — leading to the peace that culminates in nirvāṇa; yoga is for one measured in food, recreation, effort, sleep and waking. (4) 6.18–23: the state of yoga: restrained thought (citta) resting in the self alone, steady like a lamp in a windless place; thought (citta) stilled (niruddha), the self seen by the self, boundless happiness beyond the senses, no gain counted higher, not shaken even by heavy sorrow — this is to be known as yoga, the unyoking from union with sorrow, to be practised with resolve and an undejected mind (cetas). (5) 6.24–28: the method: abandoning desires born of intention and restraining the senses, coming to rest little by little with an intellect held firm, making the mind abide in the self and thinking of nothing, bringing the restless mind back whenever it wanders; the result: supreme happiness, becoming Brahman, the boundless happiness of contact with Brahman. (6) 6.29–32: the yoked one sees the self in all beings and all beings in the self; whoever sees the Lord everywhere and everything in him is not lost to him; the yogin established in oneness who worships him as abiding in all beings abides in him however he lives; the highest yogin sees pleasure and pain everywhere by likeness to himself. (7) 6.33–36: Arjuna objects that the mind is too restless for this yoga of sameness to stand steady; the Lord grants that it is hard to restrain but says it is held by practice (abhyāsa) and dispassion (vairāgya), and that yoga is attainable by the self-controlled who strive by the right means. (8) 6.37–45: Arjuna asks the fate of the one with faith who does not strive and falls from yoga; the Lord answers that no doer of good comes to a bad end: he dwells in the worlds of the meritorious, is reborn among the pure and prosperous or, more rarely, among wise yogins, regains the understanding of his former body, is carried on by former practice, and, perfected over many births, reaches the highest goal. (9) 6.46–47: the yogin is greater than ascetics, knowers and performers of works, so Arjuna should be a yogin; and of all yogins the one who worships the Lord with faith, his inner self gone into him, is the most yoked. Purpose, as the chapter presents it: to set out the discipline of meditative yoga — its prerequisites, method, state and result — to reassure the practitioner about restlessness and failure, and to place faithful worship of the Lord at the summit of yoga.

paraphrase: Chapter 7 moves in eight steps. (1) 7.1–3: with his mind attached to the Lord, practising yoga and taking refuge in him, Arjuna will know him entirely (samagram) and without doubt; the Lord will declare knowledge together with vijñāna, after which nothing further remains to be known; among thousands scarcely one strives for perfection, and of those who strive scarcely one knows him in truth. (2) 7.4–7: his two natures — the lower, divided eightfold (earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, intellect and the sense of 'I'), and the higher, which has become the living being and by which the world is upheld; all beings have these two as their womb; he is the origin and the dissolution of the whole world; nothing is higher than him, and all this is strung on him like gems on a thread. (3) 7.8–12: he is the essence in things — the taste in water, the light of moon and sun, Oṃ in all the Vedas, sound in space, manhood in men, fragrance in earth, brilliance in fire, life in all beings, austerity in ascetics, the eternal seed of beings, the intelligence of the intelligent, the strength of the strong free of desire and passion, desire not opposed to dharma; the states of sattva, rajas and tamas come from him, yet he is not in them — they are in him. (4) 7.13–15: deluded by these guṇa-made states the world does not know him; his divine māyā made of the guṇas is hard to cross, but those who take refuge in him alone cross it; evil-doers of demonic disposition, their knowledge carried off by māyā, do not take refuge in him. (5) 7.16–19: four kinds of people of good deeds worship him — the distressed, the one who wishes to know, the seeker of gain and the knower; all are noble, but the knower, ever yoked and of single devotion, is foremost, mutually dear with him and held by him to be his very self; at the end of many births the knower takes refuge in him, knowing 'Vāsudeva is all' — a great soul very hard to find. (6) 7.20–23: those whose knowledge desires have carried off resort to other deities, following their observances; whatever form a devotee wishes to worship with faith, he makes that faith firm, and through it the worshipper obtains desires ordained by him; but the fruit is finite — worshippers of the gods go to the gods, his devotees come to him. (7) 7.24–26: the unintelligent think of him as unmanifest come into manifestation, not knowing his higher, imperishable state; veiled by his yoga-māyā he is not manifest to all; he knows all beings past, present and to come, but no one knows him. (8) 7.27–30: all beings fall into bewilderment at birth through the delusion of the pairs born of desire and aversion; those of meritorious deeds whose sin has ended worship him firm in their vows; those who take refuge in him and strive for release from old age and death know Brahman, the adhyātma and action completely, and those who know him with the adhibhūta, the adhidaiva and the adhiyajña know him even at the time of departure — terms that Arjuna asks about in 8.1–2. Purpose, as the chapter presents it: to give the knowledge of the Lord 'entire' (samagra), together with vijñāna, and to show refuge in him as the way across his māyā.

paraphrase: Chapter 8 moves in nine steps. (1) 8.1–2: Arjuna asks seven questions — what is that Brahman, what is the adhyātma, what is action, what are the adhibhūta and the adhidaiva, who and how is the adhiyajña here in the body, and how is the Lord to be known at the time of departure by the self-controlled. (2) 8.3–4: the Lord's answers: Brahman is the supreme imperishable; own being (svabhāva) is called the adhyātma; the sending-forth (visarga) that brings about beings' states of existence is called action; the adhibhūta is the perishable state, the adhidaivata puruṣa ('person'), and the adhiyajña the Lord himself, here in the body. (3) 8.5–8: whoever departs at the end remembering him alone comes to his state; one goes to whatever state one remembers on leaving the body, having always been shaped by it; therefore Arjuna is to remember him at all times and fight, with mind and intellect offered to him; with thought (cetas) yoked by the yoga of repeated practice one goes to the supreme divine Person. (4) 8.9–13: the departure of one who remembers: whoever at departure, with unmoving mind, devotion and the power of yoga, the breath made to enter between the brows, remembers the ancient seer, subtler than the subtle, sun-coloured, beyond darkness, reaches that supreme divine Person; the imperishable that knowers of the Veda speak of and ascetics enter is declared in brief: whoever departs having restrained the gates, confined the mind in the heart and placed the breath in the head, uttering Oṃ, the one-syllabled Brahman, and remembering him, goes to the supreme goal. (5) 8.14–16: for the ever-yoked yogin who remembers him constantly with thought on nothing else (ananya-cetas) he is easy to reach; the great souls who come to him are not reborn into the impermanent abode of sorrow, whereas all worlds up to Brahmā's are subject to return. (6) 8.17–19: Brahmā's day lasts a thousand yugas and his night as long; at the coming of day manifest things come forth from the unmanifest, at the coming of night they dissolve into it, and the same multitude of beings comes to be again and again, helplessly. (7) 8.20–22: beyond that unmanifest is another, eternal unmanifest being that does not perish when all beings perish; it is called the imperishable and the supreme goal, from which they do not return — his supreme abode; that supreme Person, in whom beings abide and by whom all is pervaded, is gained by undivided devotion. (8) 8.23–27: the times at which departing yogins go to non-return or to return: fire, light, day, the bright fortnight and the six months of the northern course lead the knowers of Brahman to Brahman; smoke, night, the dark fortnight and the six months of the southern course lead the yogin to the lunar light and return; these two courses are everlasting for the world, and knowing them no yogin is deluded — so Arjuna is to be yoked in yoga at all times. (9) 8.28: having known this, the yogin goes beyond all the merit declared for the Vedas, sacrifices, austerities and gifts and reaches the supreme, primal place. Purpose, as the chapter presents it: to answer the questions left open at 7.29–30, above all how the Lord is known at death, and to show that constant remembrance of him, carried through to the moment of departure, leads to the imperishable from which there is no return.

paraphrase: Chapter 9 moves in nine steps. (1) 9.1–3: to Arjuna, who does not cavil, the Lord will declare the most secret knowledge together with vijñāna, knowing which he will be freed from what is inauspicious — the royal knowledge, the royal secret, the supreme purifier, directly apprehended, in accord with dharma, very easy to practise, imperishable; those without faith in this dharma do not reach him and return to the path of death and saṃsāra. (2) 9.4–10: all this is pervaded by him in unmanifest form; all beings abide in him, but he is not established in them — and yet beings do not abide in him: 'behold my lordly yoga'; his self sustains beings and brings them into being without abiding in them, as the great wind always abides in space; at the close of a kalpa beings go into his prakṛti and at its beginning he sends them forth again, taking hold of his own prakṛti; these acts do not bind him, seated as one indifferent and unattached; with him as overseer prakṛti gives birth to the moving and the unmoving, and so the world revolves. (3) 9.11–12: the deluded disregard him who has taken on a human body, not knowing his higher state as the great Lord of beings; of vain hopes, vain acts and vain knowledge, they resort to the deluding nature of rākṣasas and asuras. (4) 9.13–15: the great souls, resorting to the divine nature, worship him with minds on nothing else — always glorifying him, striving, firm in their vows, bowing to him with devotion, ever yoked — and others worship him by the sacrifice of knowledge, as one, as distinct and in many ways. (5) 9.16–19: he is the rite, the sacrifice, the offering to the ancestors, the healing plant, the mantra, the clarified butter, the fire and the oblation; the father, mother, sustainer and grandsire of the world, what is to be known, the purifier, Oṃ, and the Ṛk, Sāman and Yajus; the goal, upholder, lord, witness, dwelling, refuge and friend, the origin, dissolution, ground, treasure-house and imperishable seed; he gives heat, holds back and sends forth the rain; he is immortality and death, being and non-being. (6) 9.20–21: knowers of the three Vedas who have worshipped him with sacrifices pray for heaven, enjoy the world of the lord of the gods and, their merit spent, enter the world of mortals again — 'going and coming'. (7) 9.22–25: for those who, having no other, think of him and worship him, ever devoted, he himself carries acquisition and preservation; devotees of other deities who sacrifice with faith sacrifice to him, but not according to the rule; not recognising him in truth as the enjoyer and lord of all sacrifices, they fall; those vowed to the gods, the ancestors or the spirits go to them, and those who sacrifice to him come to him. (8) 9.26–28: a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water offered with devotion he partakes of; whatever Arjuna does, eats, offers, gives or practises as austerity is to be done as an offering to him, and so he will be freed from the bonds of action with their good and bad fruits and, yoked in the yoga of renunciation, will come to him. (9) 9.29–34: he is the same to all beings, none hateful or dear to him, but those who worship him with devotion are in him and he in them; even one of very bad conduct who worships him with undivided devotion is to be considered good and quickly becomes righteous — his devotee does not perish; those who take refuge in him, even those of sinful birth, women, vaiśyas and śūdras, go to the highest goal, how much more holy brāhmaṇas and devoted royal seers; closing injunction: having come to this impermanent, joyless world, worship him — mind on him, his devotee, sacrificing to him, bowing to him — and Arjuna will come to him. Purpose, as the chapter presents it: to declare the knowledge together with vijñāna (the phrase of 7.2) as the 'royal knowledge, royal secret' — the Lord who pervades all this and yet is not contained in it — and to present devotion to him, open to all who take refuge, as the way to him.

paraphrase: The thesis of the Bhagavad Gītā as its own six marks of purport (ṣaḍ-liṅga) show it, stated in the text's words; how the traditions construe these words is recorded in the notes and in dsp:gita-primary-teaching and is not decided here. (1) Opening and closing (upakrama–upasaṃhāra). The frame opens with Dhṛtarāṣṭra's question about the field of dharma (1.1) and closes with Sañjaya's verdict (18.74–78). The teaching opens on Arjuna's grief (śoka; 1.47, 2.8) and his request: his nature struck by the fault of pitiable weakness (kārpaṇya) and his thought (cetas) bewildered about dharma, he asks what is decisively better (śreyas … niścitam), as a disciple who has taken refuge (prapanna, 2.7), and says 'I will not fight' (2.9); Kṛṣṇa's first word is 'you grieve for those not to be grieved for' (2.11). The close answers it point by point: 'do not grieve' (mā śucaḥ, 18.66; also 16.5) answers 2.11; 'go to me alone for refuge' (18.66, after 'go to him alone for refuge', 18.62) answers 'prapanna' (2.7); 'abandoning all dharmas' (18.66) and the destroyed 'delusion born of ignorance' (18.72–73) answer the bewilderment about dharma (2.7); Kṛṣṇa quotes 'I will not fight' back (18.59), and Arjuna ends 'I will do your word' (18.73). (2) Repetition (abhyāsa): action without attachment to its fruit (2.47–48, 3.19, 4.20, 5.10–12, 6.1, 12.11–12, 17.11, 18.6, 18.9–11); the imperishable embodied one, who is not slain and is not the agent (2.12–30, 3.27, 5.8–9, 13.30, 14.19, 18.16–17); taking refuge in the Lord and devotion to 'me alone' (7.14, 8.14, 9.22, 9.34, 11.54, 12.2–8, 14.26, 15.19, 18.56, 18.62, 18.65–66; 18.65a repeats 9.34a); sameness toward pleasure and pain and toward all beings (2.48, 5.18–19, 6.29, 12.13–19, 14.24–25, 18.54); the guṇas as what acts and binds (3.27–29, 14.5–27, 17.2–22, 18.19–40). (3) Novelty (apūrvatā), as the text marks it: a lost yoga given again as 'the highest secret' (4.1–3), the 'royal secret' known directly (9.1–2), a form 'not seen before' (11.47–48), 'the most secret teaching' (15.20); at the close a graded mark — 'more secret than the secret' (18.63), then 'hear again my supreme word, the most secret of all' (18.64) — set on 18.65–66. (4) Stated result (phala): peace, the nirvāṇa of brahman and freedom from the bondage of action and of birth, coming to the Lord and the eternal place by his grace (2.39, 2.51, 2.71–72, 4.9, 5.24–26, 8.15–16, 9.34, 14.20, 18.56, 18.62, 18.65–66); and the result shown in the story itself: 'delusion is destroyed, memory regained through your grace; I stand firm, my doubts gone; I will do your word' (18.73). (5) Praise and blame (arthavāda): the teaching and its transmission are praised (9.2, 15.20, 18.68–71), Sañjaya praises the dialogue (18.74–78), and the demonic are blamed at length (16.7–20); as marks of purport these urge the teaching; whether particular verses are praise only (P7-arthavāda) is not decided here (see notes). (6) Reasoned demonstration (upapatti): from the nature of the embodied one (2.12–30); no one can remain without action (3.5, 18.11); the guṇas act and the self is not the agent (3.27–29, 13.30, 18.13–17); Arjuna's own nature will compel him (18.59–60); the Lord in the heart moves all beings, therefore go to him for refuge (18.61–62). By these marks the Gītā's purport is a teaching that removes Arjuna's grief and his delusion about dharma and brings him to act at Kṛṣṇa's word (2.7–11 → 18.66, 18.72–73), through knowledge of the embodied one who is not slain and does not act (2.19–21, 13.30, 13.32), action done as one's own dharma without attachment to its fruit and offered to the Lord (2.47, 3.30, 9.27–28, 18.46, 18.57), and knowing the Lord and taking refuge in him with devotion (7.14, 11.54, 18.55, 18.62, 18.66), by whose grace the eternal place is reached. The text itself once gives these an order — own work offered as worship, the perfection of freedom from action, the discipline that makes one fit for becoming brahman, supreme devotion, knowing and entering the Lord (18.45–55) — and says that the one who takes refuge in him reaches the eternal place even while acting (18.56); it closes on the word it marks as 'the most secret of all' (18.64): 'be one whose mind is on me, my devotee, one who sacrifices to me; bow to me … abandoning all dharmas, go to me alone for refuge; I will release you from all sins; do not grieve' (18.65–66). The marks do not settle what 'abandoning all dharmas' means, or which of these means is the final and direct one: there the traditions divide.
translation_basis: the merger's statement of the six marks, made from the Sanskrit text and the merged teachings of chs. 1–18; no published translation consulted

fidelity.note: Checked every cited verse in chs. 1–18 against the segments (2.7, 2.8, 2.9, 2.11, 3.35, 4.1–3, 9.1–2, 9.34, 11.47–48, 15.20, 18.59, 18.63–66, 18.72–73 and the rest): each mark is cited correctly. It states what the six marks point to in the text's words, records the traditions only in labelled notes, and says the marks do not settle 'abandoning all dharmas' or which means is final: it chooses no tradition's thesis. One clause went beyond the marks: praise and blame 'are not counted as separate doctrines' decides the P7-arthavāda question that its own notes list as 'not decided' (18.68–71, 18.78). Fixed — paraphrase: 'these urge the teaching and are not counted as separate doctrines.' -> 'as marks of purport these urge the teaching; whether particular verses are praise only (P7-arthavāda) is not decided here (see notes).'

notes: Written by the merger of the last chunk (role M, Part 7 step 4) from the merged six-marks notes of chs. 1–15 and extractors A and B's notes on chs. 16–18; every mark is cited by this edition's verse numbers (ch. 13 has the extra opening verse). The traditions draw different theses from the same marks — above all the opening 2.11 and the close 18.66 — as recorded in dsp:gita-primary-teaching (positions recalled, not checked against the bhāṣyas; to be checked in Wave 2): Advaita (Śaṅkara; Madhusūdana Sarasvatī): liberation by knowledge of the self alone, steadfastness in knowledge preceded by the renunciation of all works, action done as an offering purifying the mind for it; 18.66 read as renouncing all works, dharma and adharma alike, and resting in the Lord as the self; Madhusūdana's three hexads (action 1–6, devotion 7–12, knowledge 13–18). Viśiṣṭādvaita (Yāmuna's Gītārthasaṅgraha; Rāmānuja): Nārāyaṇa, the supreme brahman, reached by bhakti-yoga, which karma-yoga and jñāna-yoga prepare; 18.66 read as giving up the sense of agency, possession and fruit within all the yogas, or, for one unable to begin bhakti-yoga, as refuge in place of the other means; in the Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition 18.66 is the carama-śloka, the charter of prapatti. Dvaita (Madhva): the supremacy of Viṣṇu and the eternal difference of the selves; liberation by his grace through devotion grounded in knowledge of his supremacy, with desireless action as worship (15.16–18, 18.46). Abhinavagupta (Kashmir Śaiva; low confidence in data/): knowledge and action together — the one established in knowledge acts and is not bound (18.17, 4.18). Bhāskara (Bhedābheda; low confidence): knowledge combined with works (3.20). Gauḍīya (Viśvanātha Cakravartin, Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa): pure devotion to Kṛṣṇa, the most secret teaching (9.34, 18.64–66). Recent (B. G. Tilak): energetic action by the one who knows, for the welfare of the world (5.2, 3.25). The dispute's recorded reconciliation (P3 path, P4 stage, P8 six marks; partially reconciled) claims only that the text addresses different temperaments and stages; which means is final and direct is not yet reconciled. This entry states what the text's own marks point to, in the text's words, and chooses none of these theses. Candidates for the praise principle (P7-arthavāda), flagged by the chunk mergers and not decided: 4.36, 5.2, 6.46, 12.12, 13.24, 13.26, 18.68–71, 18.78. Novelty was weighed two ways in the chs. 1–3 merge: against ordinary knowledge and the ritual view (A) and against the Upaniṣads, which the Gītā often echoes (B: 2.19–20 ≈ Kaṭha 1.2.18–19, 3.42 ≈ Kaṭha 1.3.10, the aśvattha of 15.1 ≈ Kaṭha 2.3.1); the entry cites the text's own marks of novelty, its marks of secrecy. The order of 18.45–55 (devotion after becoming brahman) and the place of 18.56 (refuge while acting: a further stage or a parallel route) are read differently by the traditions (dsp:is-knowledge-the-means-of-bhakti, dsp:bhakti-jnana-precedence).
